newsitem.title: ALBANIA: One dead after violent clashes in Albanian city.
newsitem.headline: One dead after violent clashes in Albanian city.

text.p: One person died and at least 40 were injured in clashes between anti-government protesters and police in the southern Albanian port of Vlore on Sunday, officials said.

It was the bloodiest incident in the Balkan state since trouble flared last month over the collapse of pyramid savings schemes, with many people blaming President Sali Berisha and his right-wing government for the growing financial crisis.

A doctor at a Vlore hospital said a man in his 40s died of a heart attack after an angry crowd had pelted the city's main police station with stones and security forces responded by firing shots into the air.
Demonstrators said the man was covered with blood when he was rushed to hospital and blamed police for his death.
The doctor said many of the injured had minor buckshot wounds and one person was in intensive care. State radio said 22 people were hurt, including a policeman.
Widespread rioting swept Albania in January after hugely popular pyramid schemes started to go bust, leaving thousands of families destitute.

The protests were capped by a swift police crackdown and nationwide arrests. Disturbances erupted again last week after a pyramid scheme based in Vlore went bankrupt owing investors a staggering $500 million.
Police initially tried to halt rallies in the Adriatic port, 140 km (80 miles) south of Tirana, but were overwhelmed by the sheer number of protesters.
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets, demanding refunds for money lost in the pyramid scams and Sunday marked the fifth consecutive day of demonstrations in the city.

Crowds marched on a central police station at sundown after rumours spread that people had been arrested. City authorities cut off electricity to the area, leaving streets in darkness and demonstrators later dispersed.

The official ATA news agency said President Berisha met a politicians from Vlore on Sunday who called on the government to help people who sold their homes to invest the cash in the pyramids and declare the area an economic free zone.
ATA said Berisha pledged to help investors left penniless by the scandal and called on Albanians to shun violence.
Many people blame the ruling Democratic Party, founded by Berisha, of doing nothing to stop the dramatic spread of pyramid funds in post-communist Albania.
Riot police prevented opposition parties from staging anti-government rallies in Tirana on Saturday, striking opposition leaders and reporters with batons and sweeping bystanders off the streets.
The Forum for Democracy, an opposition alliance which groups 10 parties, called on supporters on Sunday to offer passive resistance to the state.

"The Forum calls on the people to demonstrate peacefully every day from 12 p.m. to 2 p.m in any form," it said in a statement printed in Tirana newspapers. "Gather silently on pavements, demonstrate with a slice of bread in your hand, close down shops, boycott classrooms, sound your car horns."

The leader of the centre-right Democratic Alliance party, Neritan Ceka, was punched around the head by men wearing khaki uniforms in a central Tirana bar. He said they had been hired by the ruling party.
"It reminded me of the Nazis. I think we are living in the same period now. It is terrible," he told Reuters.
